8d72ed3606: This chapter builds five ideas carefully, with runnable examples for each. First, how code gets run and how names attach to objects. Then the built-in types, what counts as true, and how control flows through a program. By the end you will read Python the way the interpreter reads it. The surprises in later chapters will be far fewer.
91e492d5c2: The confusion it resolves sounds like this: "I assigned a list to a new variable, changed the new variable, and the old one changed too." That behavior is not a bug. It follows directly from how assignment works. Once you see it, you will predict it every time.
db098d6b48: Two flags extend the REPL's reach. python3.13 -i script.py runs the script and then drops you into an interactive session with all its names still alive. That is handy for inspecting what a script built. python3.13 -c "print(2 + 3)" runs a one-liner without a file.
1628c5a8a7: The standard library is the same mechanism at scale: hundreds of modules ship with every Python. This guide uses only the standard library. Every import you see — copy, math, pathlib — works on a plain Python 3.13 install with nothing to download. That constraint is deliberate, not a limitation. The standard library covers an enormous amount of ground.
34a0e02927: The rule for is: use it for singletons, and almost nowhere else. None comes first among them. x is None is the correct None check, and for a reason beyond style. None is a singleton: exactly one None object exists. So identity is the right test, and an object with a strange __eq__ cannot fool it. (PEP 8 recommends is None for the same reason.)
728489c4ed: Do not use is to compare numbers or strings. a = 5; b = 5; a is b may be True on CPython. CPython caches small integers (-5 to 256), and it may reuse identical constants compiled together. That is an implementation detail of one interpreter, not a language promise. Another interpreter, or the same interpreter on a different day, may give False. Compare values with ==; compare identity with is. Mixing them up is a real source of bugs that only appear in production.
a5373e71cd: The mutable-default-argument trap. This chapter's model explains it, though the full story belongs to the functions chapter. A default like def f(items=[]) binds one list object at definition time, and every call shares it. Same sticky note, many calls.
44411b4050: Python is dynamically typed: names have no types, objects do. x = 3 binds x to an int object; x = "hi" rebinds the same name to a str object. The name never promised anything. This flexibility makes the type system matter more, not less. The checks happen at runtime, on the objects. So you need to know what each type guarantees.
de2847709a:
float is for measurement and scientific computing. On the platforms you will use, it is a 64-bit binary floating-point number. Binary cannot represent most decimal fractions exactly, just as decimal cannot represent 1/3. So 0.1 + 0.2 is 0.30000000000000004, not 0.3. This is not a Python bug. Binary floating point works this way everywhere. Two consequences follow:

  • Never compare floats with ==; use math.isclose(a, b) for "close enough."
  • Never use float for money. Count cents in int, or use decimal.Decimal from the standard library. (That is convention born of hard experience, not a language rule.)
289f7e037e: Two rows deserve a second look. -7 // 2 is -4, not -3. Floor division rounds toward negative infinity; it does not truncate. And -7 % 2 is 1, not -1. The result takes the divisor's sign, which keeps the invariant (a // b) * b + (a % b) == a true. If you expected C-like truncation, that expectation is the bug.
82984ded7a: A few notes on the output. s[::-1] reverses via a step of -1; slice syntax is [start:stop:step]. The f-string (f"Hello, {name}!") interpolates expressions inside braces. It is the standard way to build messages, and it beats concatenation for anything beyond the trivial. s.replace returned "heLLo" while s stayed "hello": immutability in action. in tests substring membership.
398b87967f: Two subtleties. First, (1) is just 1 with parentheses; the comma makes the tuple: (1,). Second, tuple immutability is shallow. The tuple t cannot be rebound to different items, but the list inside it can still mutate — and did. Immutability protects the container's structure, not its contents. A tuple is only deeply immutable if everything inside it is too. That is exactly why tuples of strings and numbers work as dict keys.
985809f8b8: Reading a missing key with scores["zoe"] raises KeyError. get() avoids that: it returns a default instead. Reaching for get() with a sensible default is the standard defensive read. It exists precisely because missing keys are normal in mapping code, not exceptional.
d0f0c52021: Everything else is truthy. bool() applies these rules, and if/while apply them implicitly. So if items: means "if items is non-empty." It reads better than if len(items) > 0:, and it is the idiomatic form.
d5db1191f0: The distinction bites in two places. First, you cannot use a statement where an expression is expected. x = (if True: 1) is a SyntaxError, which is why the conditional expression (1 if True else 2) exists. Second, assignment is a statement, so if x = 5: is a SyntaxError too. Python forces you to write ==, and that closes off an entire class of C bugs. (The walrus operator :=, assignment as an expression, is the deliberate exception; later chapter.)
9eb998ad83: Order your conditions from most specific to most general. The first truthy branch wins, and later branches never run. The conditional expression a if cond else b is for small value choices, not for logic. If either branch needs more than an expression, write the full if block.
035a23812f: for iterates over items. It does not count unless you ask it to. range(3) produces 0, 1, 2 for counting, but the idiomatic loop iterates the collection directly: for name in names:. Index-obsessed loops are a habit to unlearn. If you need indices too, enumerate() pairs each item with its index.
414cbaa0a7: A comprehension builds a collection from a loop in one expression: [expr for item in items if condition]. The same shape makes sets ({...}) and dicts ({key: value ...}). A generator expression uses the same syntax with parentheses, but it builds nothing. It yields items lazily, one at a time. That is how you process large streams without materializing them.
2053278a7b: Comprehensions are for building collections from iterations. When the loop body has side effects (printing, appending to multiple structures, complex branching), write the plain loop. A comprehension with side effects reads badly and surprises readers. And when a comprehension needs two nested fors plus a condition, that is usually the signal to write the loop out. One level of nesting with a filter is the sweet spot.
091a82c3d9: 2.2 — config prints {'retries': 3, 'hosts': ['a', 'b', 'c']}. The shallow copy shares the inner list, so c2["hosts"].append("c") mutates the original's list. c2["retries"] = 5 only rebinds a key in the copy's own dict. Fix: c2 = copy.deepcopy(config). Rule: reach for deepcopy when the structure contains mutable objects that you will mutate through the copy. Once nesting is involved, one level of copying is not enough.
707fa92a2c: The multiple-of-both check comes first because 15 is also a multiple of 3. The first truthy branch wins, so an earlier % 3 check would swallow the fizzbuzz case.
